terms.grammar: preposition with the ablative; ā before consonants, ab before vowels and h
terms.comment: Separation and distance: ā mē abesse, be away from me. With names of towns, domus and rūs prose uses the ablative alone (domō abesse); verse may add ā. The prefix ab- says it in the verb: abīre, go away (see away).

terms.grammar: adverb; with ab + ablative, or the ablative alone in verse
terms.comment: Far off, out of the way: procul ab urbe; alone, as a command, procul!, away! (see far).

phrases.latin: avē, mī Gāī, meus asellus jūcundissimus, quem semper medius fidius dēsīderō, cum ā mē abes
phrases.english: greetings, my Gaius, my dearest little donkey, whom I always miss, so help me, when you are away from me

phrases.latin: longē quōs simul ā domō profectōs dīversae variē viae reportant
phrases.english: who set out together far away from home, and whom different roads bring back by different ways

phrases.latin: beātus ille quī procul negōtiīs, ut prīsca gēns mortālium
phrases.english: happy the man who, far away from business, like the first race of mortals …

phrases.latin: pōma sumus Cybelēs: procul hinc discēde, viātor, nē cadat in miserum nostra ruīna caput
phrases.english: we are Cybele’s fruit: get well away from here, traveller, or we may fall on your poor head

phrases.latin: sed tamen īra procul absit, cum quā nihil rēctē fierī, nihil cōnsīderātē potest
phrases.english: but let anger be far away, for with it nothing can be done rightly or with thought
